Joint distribution of the log-rank statistic at several calendar times

Source: R/lr_cov.R
lr_cov.Rd

Returns the mean vector and covariance matrix of the standardized log-rank statistics Z(t_1), ..., Z(t_K) of one endpoint, or of PFS and OS together.

Usage

lr_cov(
  scenario,
  n,
  calendar_time,
  endpoint = "os",
  mean = c("direct", "schoenfeld"),
  variance = c("null", "alternative", "studentized"),
  trigger = NULL
)

Arguments

scenario

An ms_scenario object.

n

Total sample size.

calendar_time

Strictly increasing calendar times (positive).

endpoint

"os", "pfs" or both (for example c("pfs", "os")).

mean

"direct" or "schoenfeld".

variance

"null", "alternative" or "studentized".

trigger

Endpoint whose observed number of events determines each calendar time ("os" or "pfs"; one value or one per time), or NULL or NA for fixed calendar times. Used only with variance = "studentized".

Value

A list with time, endpoint, events, info, mean (mean vector of Z) and sigma (covariance matrix of Z), with one element (row) per endpoint and time.

Details

With variance = "null" the statistics have unit variances and correlations sqrt(V(t_j) / V(t_k)) for t_j <= t_k, from the independent increments of the score (Tsiatis 1981). With variance = "alternative" the covariance of the score under the alternative is that of Luo et al. (2019), computed here from the per-patient influence functions of the score, and is divided by sqrt(V(t_j) V(t_k)).

With variance = "studentized" the covariance is the asymptotic covariance of Z = -U / sqrt(V-hat) itself, where V-hat is the usual variance estimator. The per-patient influence function of Z adds to that of the score a term for the variability of V-hat and, for times determined by the observed number of events of an endpoint (trigger), a term for the variability of the analysis time. Both terms vanish under the null hypothesis.

For PFS and OS together (endpoint = c("pfs", "os")) the statistics are ordered by endpoint and then by time. With "studentized" all covariances come from the influence functions. With "null" the statistics of one endpoint have the covariances described above and the correlations between the endpoints are those of the studentized statistics. With "alternative" the covariances between the endpoints are the covariances of the scores divided by sqrt(V_P V_O). Under the null hypothesis the three choices agree, and the covariance between the endpoints is that of Danzer et al. (2025, Theorem 1).

References

Tsiatis AA (1981). The asymptotic joint distribution of the efficient scores test for the proportional hazards model calculated over time. Biometrika 68:311-315.

Luo X, Mao X, Chen X, Qiu J, Bai S, Quan H (2019). Design and monitoring of survival trials in complex scenarios. Statistics in Medicine 38:192-209.

Danzer MF, Rufibach K, Beyersmann J, Schmidt R (2025). Exhausting the type I error level in event-driven group-sequential designs with a closed testing procedure for progression-free and overall survival. arXiv:2512.08658.

See also

lr_moments, gs_prob

Examples

ctl <- ms_model(death = log(2) / 12)
trt <- ms_model(death = 0.7 * log(2) / 12)
scn <- ms_scenario(ctl, trt, accrual = ms_accrual(rate = 20))
lr_cov(scn, n = 400, calendar_time = c(24, 36))
#> $time
#> [1] 24 36
#> 
#> $endpoint
#> [1] "os" "os"
#> 
#> $events
#> [1] 189.2029 281.1176
#> 
#> $info
#> [1] 47.04842 69.42161
#> 
#> $mean
#> [1] 2.446035 2.987523
#> 
#> $sigma
#>           [,1]      [,2]
#> [1,] 1.0000000 0.8232376
#> [2,] 0.8232376 1.0000000
#> 
fl <- ms_scenario(ms_fleischer(3, 9), ms_fleischer(4.3, 12.9),
                  accrual = ms_accrual(rate = 20))
lr_cov(fl, n = 400, calendar_time = 30, endpoint = c("pfs", "os"),
       variance = "studentized")
#> $time
#> [1] 30 30
#> 
#> $endpoint
#> [1] "pfs" "os" 
#> 
#> $events
#> [1] 383.8650 281.1558
#> 
#> $info
#> [1] 91.89643 69.35358
#> 
#> $mean
#> [1] 3.507546 3.015257
#> 
#> $sigma
#>          [,1]     [,2]
#> [1,] 0.983061 0.384386
#> [2,] 0.384386 0.999025
#>
